# Process controls for improving bioleaching performance of both Li and Co from spent lithium ion batteries at high pulp density and its thermodynamics and kinetics exploration

Zhirui Niu a,b, Yikan Zou a, Baoping Xin a,⇑, Shi Chen a, Changhao Liu a, Yuping Li a

\- Bioleaching behavior of spent LIBs at pulp density (PD) of 1–4% was explored.

\- Great decline in leaching efficiency was observed for Co/Li with increase in PD.

\- Maximum leach yield of 89% for Li and 72% for Co was reach by process control.

\- Bioleaching has greater potential than chemical leaching based on thermodynamics.

\- Product layer diffusion model described best bioleaching behavior of Co and Li.

## ABSTRACT

Release of Co and Li from spent lithium ion batteries (LIBs) by bioleaching has attracted growing attentions. However, the pulp density was only 1% or lower, meaning that a huge quantity of media was required for bioleaching. In this work, bioleaching behavior of the spent LIBs at pulp densities ranging from 1% to 4% was investigated and process controls to improve bioleaching performance at pulp density of 2% were explored. The results showed that the pulp density exerted a considerable influence on leaching performance of Co and Li. The bioleaching efficiency decreased respectively from 52% to 10% for Co and from 80% to 37% for Li when pulp density rose from 1% to 4%. However, the maximum extraction efficiency of 89% for Li and 72% for Co was obtained at pulp density of 2% by process controls. Bioleaching of the spent LIBs has much greater potential to occur than traditional chemical leaching based on thermodynamics analysis. The product layer diffusion model described best bioleaching behavior of Co and Li. 2014 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved.

## 1. Introduction

Lithium ion batteries (LIBs) were widely used as small power supplier owing to high energy density, no memory effect and longer life cycles (Broussely and Archdale, 2004). Not only that, LIBs will be the first category of dynamic batteries to provide power for electronic automobile in the future (Castillo et al., 2002; Xu et al., 2008). While global consumption of LIBs reached 4.49 x10 ^9 units in 2011, and the compound annual growth rate of the global consumption was as high as 14.5% from 2006 to 2011. As a consequence, massive amount of spent LIBs as solid wastes have been generated, even more in the future (Castillo et al., 2002; Xu et al., 2008).

Although spent LIBs are not classified as dangerous waste, their discharge into environment still causes potential ecosystem hazard and human health due to the toxic elements or compounds (Hal and Angelica, 2008). On the other hand, the spent LIBs contain dense valuable metals such as Co and Li in the proportion of 5– 20% cobalt and 5–7% lithium (Lee and Rhee, 2003). Under the circumstance, the huge contrast between the dense valuable metals in the LIBs and the increasing shortage of nature resource has prompted scientists to recover Co and Li in recycling spent LIBs from the viewpoints of both environment protection and resource conservation (Castillo et al., 2002; Xu et al., 2008).

Hydrometallurgical processes have been commercially adopted for recovery of Co and Li from spent LIBs (Swain et al., 2007; Li et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2009; Ferreira et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2012). However, their inherent drawbacks including stringent requirements of equipments, hard operation conditions and great energy consumption make it urgent to look for alternative strategies (Castillo et al., 2002; Xu et al., 2008). In mining, bio-hydrometallurgy (bioleaching) has been gradually replacing hydrometallurgical ones due to higher efficiency, lower costs, green process and few industrial requirements (Rohwerder et al., 2003; Cui and Zhang, 2008). Lately, extraction of Co and Li from spent LIBs by bioleaching has obtained increasing attentions (Mishra et al., 2008a; Xin et al., 2009; Zeng et al., 2012).

Pulp density is a very important factor which determines commercial application of bioleaching to some degree. An increase in pulp density from 1% to 2% (w/v) means a sharp reduction of 50% in both quantity of leaching media and size of bioreactor, resulting in a great drop in bioleaching cost. In bio-hydrometallurgy of lowgrades ores, the pulp density is generally 10% or higher (Rohwerder et al., 2003). In contrast, the optimizing pulp density was only 1% or lower with spent LIBs possibly thanks to the toxic electrolyte (Mishra et al., 2008a; Xin et al., 2009; Zeng et al., 2012), keeping the promising biotechnology away from its practical application.

In this work, bioleaching of spent LIBs at higher pulp density of 2% or above was explored. The goals of this study were (i) to analyze the bioleaching performance of Co and Li from spent LIBs when pulp density varied from 1% to 4%; (ii) to assess the feasibility to improve bioleaching efficiency of Co and Li at pulp density of 2% based on process controls; (iii) to probe the bioleaching thermodynamics and dynamics of Co and Li at pulp density of 2%; and (iv) to expound the bioleaching microprocess of Co and Li at pulp density of 2% using XRD and SEM.

## 2. Materials and methods

## 2.1. Preparing spent LIBs powder and determining content ofLi and Co

The spent LIBs were manually dismantled into different portions including plastic shell, cathode, anode, aluminum foil and so on. Then the separated active cathode and anode containing dense Co and Li were mixed, ground by milling and sieved to obtain a mesh size of less than 200 lm (Mishra et al., 2008a). The resulting powder, used for bioleaching experiments, was digested by HF - HNO _ 3 –HCl method (USEPA, 1996) to determine the content of Co at 358 mg g ^-1 and Li at 45 mg g ^-1 using AAS.

## 2.2. Acclimation of LIBs-tolerant bacteria and media

The Alicyclobacillus sp. as sulfur-oxidizing bacteria (SOB) and the Sulfobacillus sp. as iron-oxidizing bacteria (IOB) were utilized for bioleaching the spent LIBs in the form of mixed culture after acclimation of 30 d by contact with the spent LIB powder at dose ranging from 0.25% to 1.0% (w/v) (higher dose of over 1.0% evidently inhibited the growth of both cells). The detailed procedures and methods about screen, culture, maintain, inoculum and identification of the SOB and IOB were described in the previous paper (Xin et al., 2011).

## 2.3. Bioleaching experiments

Bioleaching experiments were conducted according to the previous paper (Xin et al., 2009). Unless specifically stated, bioleaching media containing 4.0 g L ^-1 of mixed energy matters (sulfur and pyrite) was inoculated respectively with SOB and IOB as the mixed culture, followed by incubation at 30 C until the pH value dropped to ca 1.0 and the ORP value rose to ca 450 mV. At that time, the spent LIB powder was added into the media to a final concentration of 2% to initiate the bioleaching after its pH value was adjusted precisely to pH 1.0. Three pulp densities (1%, 2% and 4%) were set to examine bioleaching behavior of Co and Li when pulp density increased from 1% to 4%. Three doses of mixed energy substrates (2.0, 4.0 and 8.0 g L ^-1) were set to assess the feasibility of improving extraction of Co and Li by lifting energy matters dose. The pH value of the media was controlled at pH 2.0 during bioleaching by adding H2S04 to assess the possibility of suitable pH for cells growth to promote extraction of Co and Li (bioleaching dose was obtained by measured dose subtracted released one in blank flasks with addition of the same amount of exogenous H2S04). Three bioleaching temperatures (30, 35, and 40 ^∘C) were set to inspect the feasibility of rising temperature to improve performance. The suitable controls including cells-free media, pure H2S04 solution at pH 1.0, H2SO4 at t pH 1.0 + FeSO4 at 2.0 g L ^-1, H2S04 at pH 1.0 + Fe2 (SO4)3 at 2.0 g L ^-1 were run. During bioleaching, release dose of Co and Li, Fe ^2+ and Fe ^3+ dosage, pH, ORP and cell number were periodically monitored. All experiments were carried out in triplicates.

## 2.5. Bioleaching dynamics of Co and Li at different temperatures

The bioleaching kinetics of Co/Li from spent LIBs under different temperatures were compared by establishing the mathematical relationship between the fraction of Co and Li dissolved and the leaching time using various kinetic models according to Mishra et al. (2008b).

## 2.6. Apparatuses and conditions

The pH value of bioleaching media was determined using a pH meter, the ORP value was determined by portable ORP meter; the Co and Li was determined by AAS after the samples were centrifuged at 10000g for 10 min to remove the cells and solid matters. Fe ^ 2̅ + and Fe ^3+ dosage were measured by spectrophotometry (Harvey et al., 1955). The cell number of the mixed culture was counted using a microscope after the samples were treated by ultrasonic to release the adherent bacteria. Structure change analysis was performed by XRD. Morphology variation of the spent LIB powder after bioleaching was analyzed by SEM.

## 3. Result and discussion

3.1. Leaching behavior of Co and Li from spent LIBs under varied pulp densities

Pulp density displayed notable influence on bioleaching performance of both Co and Li from spent LIBs. When pulp densities increased from 1% to 4%, the bioleaching efficiency decreased from 52% to 10% for Co and from 80% to 37% for Li after a culture period of 11 d, respectively (Fig. 1). As for released dose, however, Li elevated from 360 to 660 mg L^-1;; whereas Co fell from 1862 to 1432 mg L ^-1 (Fi g. 1). On the other hand, pulp density also greatly affected variation behavior of both pH and ORP of the bioleaching media. In general, the pH value rose and ORP value dropped due to massive consumption of H ^+ for mobilization of both Co and Li (Fi g. 2). Further, it was found that higher pulp density resulted in higher pH value and lower ORP value. With increase of the pulp density from 1% to 4%, pH value increased from 1.97 to 4.46 and ORP value decreased from 509 to 335 mV after incubation of 11 d, respectively (Fig. 2). By contrast, the sterile control kept no dissolution of Li and Co throughout bioleaching; of the three chemical leaching controls, H2SO4 + FeSO4 harvested the maximum Co yield (9%) and H2S04 + Fe2 (S04)3 obtained the maximum Li efficiency (17%) at 2% of pulp density.

In the past studies, Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans only as IOB was used for leaching spent LIBs (Mishra et al., 2008a; Zeng et al., 2012). In the case of 1% sulfur + 3 gL ^-1 ferrous as the mixed energy substrates, 56% of Co dissolution and 8% of Li release were attained at pulp density of 1% after 20 d culture, in which a possible reduction of insoluble Co^3+ into soluble Co^2+ by unknown intermediate reducing compounds which might come from sulfur metabolism was put forward as bioleaching mechanism (Mishra et al., 2008a). In the case of ferrous at 9 g L ^-1 as sole energy substrates, 43% of Co extraction was achieved after 10 d of culture at 1% of pulp density (Zeng et al., 2012). However, the Co release rose up to 99% in the presence of copper catalysis and a completely different mechanism regarding Co extraction was proposed that formulate as following (Zeng et al., 2012):

4 LiCoO2 + 12 H ^+ →4 Li ^+ + 4 Co ^2+ + 6 H2O + O2 ↑ (Eq. 5)

High pulp density could significantly reduce the amount of bioleaching media and the bioleaching cost. The bioleaching performance of the mixed culture was assessed at high pulp densities of more than 1%, and an evident decline in bioleaching efficiency was observed for both Co and Li with increase of pulp density from 1% to 4% (Fig. 1). The spent LIBs contained not only LiCoO2 as electrode but also toxic and flammable electrolyte, an organic liquid with dissolved substances like LiClO4, LiBF4 and LiPF6 (Xu et al., 2008). At higher pulp density, much more amount of toxic electrolyte was dissolved into bioleaching media, endangering the growth and activity of both kinds of bacteria in spite of spent LIBs-tolerance (Fig. 3). Lower activity of SOB resulted in less generation of H2S04 and thereby higher pH value of media; lower activities of IOB led to less amount of Fe ^ 3̅ + and thereby lower ORP value of media (Fig. 2). Li release mainly depended on the SOB because of acid dissolution as bioleaching mechanism; whereas Co liberation relied on both the SOB and IOB due to the combined action of both acid dissolution and Fe ^2+ mediated reduction as bioleaching mechanism (Xin et al., 2009). Therefore, great decline in bioleaching efficiency was occurred for both Co and Li when increase in pulp density (Fig. 1). In the following studies, the process controls were attempted to improve the bioleaching efficiency of Co and Li at pulp density of 2%.

## 3.2. Increasing dose of mixed energy substrate for promoting bioleaching performance at pulp density of 2%

The dose of mixed energy substrates affected bioleaching performance of spent LIBs to some degree. When concentration of the mixed energy substrate increased from 2.0 to4.0 g L ^-1, the maximum released efficiency rose from 57% to 62% for Li and from 21% to 32% for Γ0, respectively (Fig. 4). However, the higher dose of 8.0 g L^-1 did not lead to higher released efficiency of both Co and Li compared with the case of 4.0 g L ^-1, although the 8.0 g L ^-1 of dose harvested the lowest pH value due to the greatest production of H2S04 by the SOB and the highest ORP value due to the greatest

production of ferric by the IOB (Fig. 4). The results showed that 4̅. 0 g L ^-1 of mixed energy substrates was sufficient for mobilization of both Co and Li from the spent LIBs at pulp density of 2%.

3.3. Improving bioleaching performance ofspent LIBs at pulp density of 2% by acid adjustment of media during bioleaching

Acid adjustment during bioleaching evidently improved the extraction of both Co and Li from spent LIBs. Remarkable increase of bioleaching efficiency from 62% to 78% for Li and from 31% to 52% for Co was achieved after culture of 11 d by acid adjustment (Fig. 5). In the case of acid adjustment, the pH value of bioleaching media was kept at around 2.0 which were suitable to the growth and activity of the leaching cells, especially the IOB which generated more amount of ferric, resulting in higher ORP value than the case of no adjustment (Fig. 5). Therefore, increase of 16% for Li and 21% for Co occurred owing to acid adjustment.

## 3.4. Improving bioleaching performance ofspent LIBs at pulp density of 2% by increasing bioleaching temperature

Temperature had a strong influence on the bioleaching performance of spent LIBs. When temperature increase from 30 to 35 ^∘𝖢,, released efficiency increased from 78% to 89% for Li and from 52% to 72% for Γ0, respectively (Fig. SM-1). However, higher temperature of 40 ^∘C adversely affected the activity and growth of the leaching cells because of the mesophilic nature, leading to the lowest ORP value and Fe ^3+ / Fe ^2+ (Fig. SM-2) as well as cell density (Fig. SM-3) which accounted for the lowest mobilization doses of Co and Li (Fig. SM-1). The results demonstrated that 35 C of temperature was optimum for the bioleaching of spent LIBs. By increasing the bioleaching temperature, adding the dose of mixed energy substrates and acid adjustment of media at pH 2.0, the bioleaching efficiency of both Co and Li was notably improved and the maximum extraction efficiency of 89% for Li and 72% for Co was obtained at pulp density of 2%, respectively, indicating the great potential of process controls to promote the bioleaching performance of spent LIBs. Nevertheless, higher extraction efficiency of more than 90% for both Co and Li at higher pulp density of over 2% (even 10%) was still a challenge, which was expected for the practical application. Changing the structure of LiCoO2 by pretreatments such as ultrasound, microwave and heat as well as acclimating high tolerant-electrolytes leaching strain was alternatives to further improve bioleaching performance of spent LIBs in the future studied.

## 3.5. Bioleaching thermodynamics of Co and Li from the spent LIBs

The bioleaching mechanism of Co and Li from the spent LIBs was described as the following equation which was mentioned at previous work (Xin et al., 2009):

10 O2 + S + 2 FeS2 + 2 LiCoO2 = Li2SO4 + 2 CoSO4 + Fe2 (SO4)3 (Eq. 6)

While the mechanisms of the traditional physical–chemical leaching were described as the following equations (Xu et al., 2008):

2 FeSO4 + 2 LiCoO2 + 4 H2SO4 = Fe2 (SO4)3 + 2 CoSO4 + Li2SO4 + 4 H2O (Eq. 7)

3 H2O2 + 2 LiCoO2 + 3 H2SO4 = 2 O2 ↑+ 2 CoSO4 + Li2SO4 + 6 H2O (Eq. 8)

The bioleaching thermodynamics of both Co and Li from LiCoO2 using elemental sulfur and pyrite as mixed energy substrates were calculated and compared with those of the traditional chemical leaching in the presence of 2 SO4 + FeSO4 / H2O2 (Table 1). The huge negative value of DG with bioleaching, being 12.7 / 11.4 times higher than that of traditional chemical leaching with FeSO4 / H2O2 as reactants, respectively, suggested that the bioleaching has much greater potential to occur spontaneously than chemical leaching, although its reaction speed is very low due to the solid nature of both sulfur and pyrite if without the help of leaching cells. However, it is the mixed culture as biocatalyst that accelerated drastically the reaction process in which solid sulfur and pyrite acted as reactants, realizing efficient dissolution of both Li and Co from spent LIBs.

The huge negative value of both DH and DS with the bioleaching demonstrated that the reaction is exothermic chemical one. As a result, higher temperature is not conductive to the reaction, as shown also in the slight decline in DG values with increase of reaction temperature. However, the bioleaching performance mostly depended on the activity of bioleaching cells. When temperature increased from 30 to 35 ^∘𝖢, the growth and activity of cells were improved correspondingly, enhancing the leaching of Li and Co; whereas further increase from 35 to 40 C adversely affected the growth and activity of cells as mesophilic bacteria, leading to a drop in bioleaching efficiency of both Co and Li.

## 3.6. Bioleaching dynamics of both Co and Li at pulp density of 2%

Four kinds of kinetics models, i.e. diffusion controlled model, chemical reaction controlled model, shrinking sphere model (Stokes regime) and product layer diffusion model (Mishra et al., 2008b), were use to describe the bioleaching behavior of both Li and Co from spent LIBs under the optimum conditions at pulp density of 2% (Table SM-1). Although all the four models could described well the bioleaching behavior of both Li and Co (R ^2 > 0.9) the product layer diffusion model fitted best due to the highest correlation coefficients. However, the intrinsic mechanisms accounting for the phenomenon was unclear.

## 3.7. Bioleaching mechanisms of Co and Li at pulp density of 2%

The bioleaching residual of the spent LIBs was analyzed using SEM and XRD and compared with the raw ones in order to reveal the bioleaching microcosmic mechanism. It was clear that the surface of spent LIBs particles grew rough and the boundary grew obscure (Fig. SM-4), indicating the occurrence of bioleaching. However, the particles did not disappear after bioleaching, accounting for remaining of Li and Co. The XRD analysis displayed that Li and Co existed in the form of LiCoO2 crystal in the raw spent LIBs, and the remaining Li and Co existed still in the form of LiCoO crystal after bioleaching (Fig. SM-5).

Despite different chemical mechanisms accounting for bioleaching of spent LIBs, there were no reports on the dynamics, thermodynamics and micro-process of the bioleaching so far. The present works demonstrated that bioleaching of spent LIBs using elemental sulfur and pyrite as mixed energy substrates has much greater potential to occur spontaneously than traditional chemical leaching in the presence of H2S04 + FeSO4 / H2O2 for the first time based on thermodynamics analysis, and the product layer diffusion model described best the bioleaching behavior of both Co and Li from the spent LIBs. Accompanying with bioleaching, spent LIBs particles grew rough in the surface and the boundary grew obscure; however, the particles did not disappear after bioleaching.

## 4. Conclusions

Pulp density displayed notable influence on bioleaching performance of Co and Li from spent LIBs. The bioleaching efficiencies decreased respectively from 52% to 10% for Co and from 80% to 37% for Li when pulp densities increased from 1% to 4%. The maximum extraction efficiency of 89% for Li and 72% for Co was obtained at pulp density of 2% through process controls. The bioleaching of spent LIBs has greater potential to occur spontaneously than traditional chemical leaching based on thermodynamics analysis. The product layer diffusion model described best the bioleaching behavior of Co and Li from the spent LIBs.

records.content: Bioleaching of Co and Li from spent LIB powder using a mixed culture of SOB (Alicyclobacillus sp.) and IOB (Sulfobacillus sp.) acclimated for 30 d with 0.25–1.0% (w/v) LIB powder. Media contained 4.0 g/L mixed energy substrates (sulfur and pyrite), incubated at 30 °C until pH ~1.0 and ORP ~450 mV, then spent LIB powder added to 2% (w/v) final concentration after adjusting pH to 1.0. Varied pulp density (1%, 2%, 4%), energy substrate dose (2.0, 4.0, 8.0 g/L), pH control (pH 2.0 by H2SO4 addition), and temperature (30, 35, 40 °C). Controls: cells-free media, pure H2SO4 at pH 1.0, H2SO4 pH 1.0 + FeSO4 2.0 g/L, H2SO4 pH 1.0 + Fe2(SO4)3 2.0 g/L. All in triplicates.

## 2.3. Bioleaching experiments
Bioleaching experiments were conducted according to the previous paper (Xin et al., 2009). Unless specifically stated, bioleaching media containing 4.0 g L ^-1 of mixed energy matters (sulfur and pyrite) was inoculated respectively with SOB and IOB as the mixed culture, followed by incubation at 30 C until the pH value dropped to ca 1.0 and the ORP value rose to ca 450 mV. At that time, the spent LIB powder was added into the media to a final concentration of 2% to initiate the bioleaching after its pH value was adjusted precisely to pH 1.0. Three pulp densities (1%, 2% and 4%) were set to examine bioleaching behavior of Co and Li when pulp density increased from 1% to 4%. Three doses of mixed energy substrates (2.0, 4.0 and 8.0 g L ^-1) were set to assess the feasibility of improving extraction of Co and Li by lifting energy matters dose. The pH value of the media was controlled at pH 2.0 during bioleaching by adding H2S04 to assess the possibility of suitable pH for cells growth to promote extraction of Co and Li (bioleaching dose was obtained by measured dose subtracted released one in blank flasks with addition of the same amount of exogenous H2S04). Three bioleaching temperatures (30, 35, and 40 ^∘C) were set to inspect the feasibility of rising temperature to improve performance. The suitable controls including cells-free media, pure H2S04 solution at pH 1.0, H2SO4 at t pH 1.0 + FeSO4 at 2.0 g L ^-1, H2S04 at pH 1.0 + Fe2 (SO4)3 at 2.0 g L ^-1 were run. During bioleaching, release dose of Co and Li, Fe ^2+ and Fe ^3+ dosage, pH, ORP and cell number were periodically monitored. All experiments were carried out in triplicates.

text_chunk.text:
## 3. Result and discussion
3.1. Leaching behavior of Co and Li from spent LIBs under varied pulp densities
Pulp density displayed notable influence on bioleaching performance of both Co and Li from spent LIBs. When pulp densities increased from 1% to 4%, the bioleaching efficiency decreased from 52% to 10% for Co and from 80% to 37% for Li after a culture period of 11 d, respectively (Fig. 1). As for released dose, however, Li elevated from 360 to 660 mg L^-1;; whereas Co fell from 1862 to 1432 mg L ^-1 (Fi g. 1). On the other hand, pulp density also greatly affected variation behavior of both pH and ORP of the bioleaching media. In general, the pH value rose and ORP value dropped due to massive consumption of H ^+ for mobilization of both Co and Li (Fi g. 2). Further, it was found that higher pulp density resulted in higher pH value and lower ORP value. With increase of the pulp density from 1% to 4%, pH value increased from 1.97 to 4.46 and ORP value decreased from 509 to 335 mV after incubation of 11 d, respectively (Fig. 2). By contrast, the sterile control kept no dissolution of Li and Co throughout bioleaching; of the three chemical leaching controls, H2SO4 + FeSO4 harvested the maximum Co yield (9%) and H2S04 + Fe2 (S04)3 obtained the maximum Li efficiency (17%) at 2% of pulp density.
In the past studies, Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans only as IOB was used for leaching spent LIBs (Mishra et al., 2008a; Zeng et al., 2012). In the case of 1% sulfur + 3 gL ^-1 ferrous as the mixed energy substrates, 56% of Co dissolution and 8% of Li release were attained at pulp density of 1% after 20 d culture, in which a possible reduction of insoluble Co^3+ into soluble Co^2+ by unknown intermediate reducing compounds which might come from sulfur metabolism was put forward as bioleaching mechanism (Mishra et al., 2008a). In the case of ferrous at 9 g L ^-1 as sole energy substrates, 43% of Co extraction was achieved after 10 d of culture at 1% of pulp density (Zeng et al., 2012). However, the Co release rose up to 99% in the presence of copper catalysis and a completely different mechanism regarding Co extraction was proposed that formulate as following (Zeng et al., 2012):
High pulp density could significantly reduce the amount of bioleaching media and the bioleaching cost. The bioleaching performance of the mixed culture was assessed at high pulp densities of more than 1%, and an evident decline in bioleaching efficiency was observed for both Co and Li with increase of pulp density from 1% to 4% (Fig. 1). The spent LIBs contained not only LiCoO2 as electrode but also toxic and flammable electrolyte, an organic liquid with dissolved substances like LiClO4, LiBF4 and LiPF6 (Xu et al., 2008). At higher pulp density, much more amount of toxic electrolyte was dissolved into bioleaching media, endangering the growth and activity of both kinds of bacteria in spite of spent LIBs-tolerance (Fig. 3). Lower activity of SOB resulted in less generation of H2S04 and thereby higher pH value of media; lower activities of IOB led to less amount of Fe ^ 3̅ + and thereby lower ORP value of media (Fig. 2). Li release mainly depended on the SOB because of acid dissolution as bioleaching mechanism; whereas Co liberation relied on both the SOB and IOB due to the combined action of both acid dissolution and Fe ^2+ mediated reduction as bioleaching mechanism (Xin et al., 2009). Therefore, great decline in bioleaching efficiency was occurred for both Co and Li when increase in pulp density (Fig. 1). In the following studies, the process controls were attempted to improve the bioleaching efficiency of Co and Li at pulp density of 2%.

The dose of mixed energy substrates affected bioleaching performance of spent LIBs to some degree. 3.3. Improving bioleaching performance ofspent LIBs at pulp density of 2% by acid adjustment of media during bioleaching
Acid adjustment during bioleaching evidently improved the extraction of both Co and Li from spent LIBs. Remarkable increase of bioleaching efficiency from 62% to 78% for Li and from 31% to 52% for Co was achieved after culture of 11 d by acid adjustment (Fig. 5). In the case of acid adjustment, the pH value of bioleaching media was kept at around 2.0 which were suitable to the growth and activity of the leaching cells, especially the IOB which generated more amount of ferric, resulting in higher ORP value than the case of no adjustment (Fig. 5). Therefore, increase of 16% for Li and 21% for Co occurred owing to acid adjustment.

text_chunk.text:
## 3.4. Improving bioleaching performance ofspent LIBs at pulp density of 2% by increasing bioleaching temperature
Temperature had a strong influence on the bioleaching performance of spent LIBs. When temperature increase from 30 to 35 ^∘𝖢,, released efficiency increased from 78% to 89% for Li and from 52% to 72% for Γ0, respectively (Fig. SM-1). However, higher temperature of 40 ^∘C adversely affected the activity and growth of the leaching cells because of the mesophilic nature, leading to the lowest ORP value and Fe ^3+ / Fe ^2+ (Fig. SM-2) as well as cell density (Fig. SM-3) which accounted for the lowest mobilization doses of Co and Li (Fig. SM-1). The results demonstrated that 35 C of temperature was optimum for the bioleaching of spent LIBs. By increasing the bioleaching temperature, adding the dose of mixed energy substrates and acid adjustment of media at pH 2.0, the bioleaching efficiency of both Co and Li was notably improved and the maximum extraction efficiency of 89% for Li and 72% for Co was obtained at pulp density of 2%, respectively, indicating the great potential of process controls to promote the bioleaching performance of spent LIBs. Nevertheless, higher extraction efficiency of more than 90% for both Co and Li at higher pulp density of over 2% (even 10%) was still a challenge, which was expected for the practical application. Changing the structure of LiCoO2 by pretreatments such as ultrasound, microwave and heat as well as acclimating high tolerant-electrolytes leaching strain was alternatives to further improve bioleaching performance of spent LIBs in the future studied.

## 3.6. Bioleaching dynamics of both Co and Li at pulp density of 2%
Four kinds of kinetics models, i.e. diffusion controlled model, chemical reaction controlled model, shrinking sphere model (Stokes regime) and product layer diffusion model (Mishra et al., 2008b), were use to describe the bioleaching behavior of both Li and Co from spent LIBs under the optimum conditions at pulp density of 2% (Table SM-1). Although all the four models could described well the bioleaching behavior of both Li and Co (R ^2 > 0.9) the product layer diffusion model fitted best due to the highest correlation coefficients. However, the intrinsic mechanisms accounting for the phenomenon was unclear.

text_chunk.text:
## 3.7. Bioleaching mechanisms of Co and Li at pulp density of 2%
The bioleaching residual of the spent LIBs was analyzed using SEM and XRD and compared with the raw ones in order to reveal the bioleaching microcosmic mechanism. It was clear that the surface of spent LIBs particles grew rough and the boundary grew obscure (Fig. SM-4), indicating the occurrence of bioleaching. However, the particles did not disappear after bioleaching, accounting for remaining of Li and Co. The XRD analysis displayed that Li and Co existed in the form of LiCoO2 crystal in the raw spent LIBs, and the remaining Li and Co existed still in the form of LiCoO crystal after bioleaching (Fig. SM-5).
Despite different chemical mechanisms accounting for bioleaching of spent LIBs, there were no reports on the dynamics, thermodynamics and micro-process of the bioleaching so far. The present works demonstrated that bioleaching of spent LIBs using elemental sulfur and pyrite as mixed energy substrates has much greater potential to occur spontaneously than traditional chemical leaching in the presence of H2S04 + FeSO4 / H2O2 for the first time based on thermodynamics analysis, and the product layer diffusion model described best the bioleaching behavior of both Co and Li from the spent LIBs. Accompanying with bioleaching, spent LIBs particles grew rough in the surface and the boundary grew obscure; however, the particles did not disappear after bioleaching.

source_evidence.quote: The Alicyclobacillus sp. as sulfur-oxidizing bacteria (SOB) and the Sulfobacillus sp. as iron-oxidizing bacteria (IOB) were utilized for bioleaching the spent LIBs in the form of mixed culture after acclimation of 30 d by contact with the spent LIB powder at dose ranging from 0.25% to 1.0% (w/v) (higher dose of over 1.0% evidently inhibited the growth of both cells). The detailed procedures and methods about screen, culture, maintain, inoculum and identification of the SOB and IOB were described in the previous paper (Xin et al., 2011).

Bioleaching experiments were conducted according to the previous paper (Xin et al., 2009). Unless specifically stated, bioleaching media containing 4.0 g L ^-1 of mixed energy matters (sulfur and pyrite) was inoculated respectively with SOB and IOB as the mixed culture, followed by incubation at 30 C until the pH value dropped to ca 1.0 and the ORP value rose to ca 450 mV. At that time, the spent LIB powder was added into the media to a final concentration of 2% to initiate the bioleaching after its pH value was adjusted precisely to pH 1.0. Three pulp densities (1%, 2% and 4%) were set to examine bioleaching behavior of Co and Li when pulp density increased from 1% to 4%. Three doses of mixed energy substrates (2.0, 4.0 and 8.0 g L ^-1) were set to assess the feasibility of improving extraction of Co and Li by lifting energy matters dose. The pH value of the media was controlled at pH 2.0 during bioleaching by adding H2S04 to assess the possibility of suitable pH for cells growth to promote extraction of Co and Li (bioleaching dose was obtained by measured dose subtracted released one in blank flasks with addition of the same amount of exogenous H2S04). Three bioleaching temperatures (30, 35, and 40 ^∘C) were set to inspect the feasibility of rising temperature to improve performance. The suitable controls including cells-free media, pure H2S04 solution at pH 1.0, H2SO4 at t pH 1.0 + FeSO4 at 2.0 g L ^-1, H2S04 at pH 1.0 + Fe2 (SO4)3 at 2.0 g L ^-1 were run. During bioleaching, release dose of Co and Li, Fe ^2+ and Fe ^3+ dosage, pH, ORP and cell number were periodically monitored. All experiments were carried out in triplicates.

records.evidence_span: The spent LIBs were manually dismantled into different portions including plastic shell, cathode, anode, aluminum foil and so on. Then the separated active cathode and anode containing dense Co and Li were mixed, ground by milling and sieved to obtain a mesh size of less than 200 lm (Mishra et al., 2008a). The resulting powder, used for bioleaching experiments, was digested by HF - HNO _ 3 –HCl method (USEPA, 1996) to determine the content of Co at 358 mg g ^-1 and Li at 45 mg g ^-1 using AAS.

evidence.quote: The spent LIBs were manually dismantled into different portions including plastic shell, cathode, anode, aluminum foil and so on. Then the separated active cathode and anode containing dense Co and Li were mixed, ground by milling and sieved to obtain a mesh size of less than 200 lm (Mishra et al., 2008a). The resulting powder, used for bioleaching experiments, was digested by HF - HNO _ 3 –HCl method (USEPA, 1996) to determine the content of Co at 358 mg g ^-1 and Li at 45 mg g ^-1 using AAS.

In this work, bioleaching behavior of the spent LIBs at pulp densities ranging from 1% to 4% was investigated and process controls to improve bioleaching performance at pulp density of 2% were explored.

final.content: Bioleaching of Co and Li from spent LIB powder using a mixed culture of SOB (Alicyclobacillus sp.) and IOB (Sulfobacillus sp.) acclimated for 30 d with 0.25–1.0% (w/v) LIB powder. Media contained 4.0 g/L mixed energy substrates (sulfur and pyrite), incubated at 30 °C until pH ~1.0 and ORP ~450 mV, then spent LIB powder added to 2% (w/v) final concentration after adjusting pH to 1.0. Varied pulp density (1%, 2%, 4%), energy substrate dose (2.0, 4.0, 8.0 g/L), pH control (pH 2.0 by H2SO4 addition), and temperature (30, 35, 40 °C). Controls: cells-free media, pure H2SO4 at pH 1.0, H2SO4 pH 1.0 + FeSO4 2.0 g/L, H2SO4 pH 1.0 + Fe2(SO4)3 2.0 g/L. All in triplicates.
final.evidence_span: Bioleaching of Co and Li from spent LIB powder using a mixed culture of SOB (Alicyclobacillus sp.) and IOB (Sulfobacillus sp.) acclimated for 30 d with 0.25–1.0% (w/v) LIB powder. Media contained 4.0 g/L mixed energy substrates (sulfur and pyrite), incubated at 30 °C until pH ~1.0 and ORP ~450 mV, then spent LIB powder added to 2% (w/v) final concentration after adjusting pH to 1.0. Varied pulp density (1%, 2%, 4%), energy substrate dose (2.0, 4.0, 8.0 g/L), pH control (pH 2.0 by H2SO4 addition), and temperature (30, 35, 40 °C).
